title: Gas Laws — Predict the Pressure
concept: Ideal gas law: how pressure responds to temperature, volume and amount
prompt: Set the sliders, watch the pressure, then commit to what happens when you change one thing at a time.
learning_objective: Predict the direction and size of the pressure change from P = nRT/V when one variable is doubled or halved.
reference: PhET Gas Properties; ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Ideal Gas Law'
note: Every prediction is checked against the ideal gas law, not against the animation: the particles show the mechanism, the equation gives the number.

spec.title: Gas Laws — Predict the Pressure
spec.instruction: Drag the sliders to explore, then pick a factor and press Check.
spec.unit_note: P = nRT/V with V in litres, T in kelvin, n in moles, R = 8.314 J/mol/K, so P is in kPa.

tasks.question: Double the temperature at constant volume. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Temperature to 600 K and leave Volume at 24.5 L.
tasks.hint: P = nRT/V. You changed a symbol that sits on the top of the fraction.
tasks.why: At constant n and V, P is directly proportional to T (Gay-Lussac's law), so doubling T doubles P: 101.8 kPa becomes 203.6 kPa.

tasks.question: Halve the volume at constant temperature. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Volume to 12.25 L and leave Temperature at 300 K.
tasks.hint: P is proportional to 1/V (Boyle's law). Squeezing the same molecules into half the space doubles how often they hit the walls.
tasks.why: Boyle's law: at constant n and T, P is inversely proportional to V, so halving V doubles P.

tasks.question: Double the amount of gas at constant temperature and volume. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Particles to 2.0 mol, keeping T = 300 K and V = 24.5 L.
tasks.hint: Twice as many molecules strike the walls in the same time.
tasks.why: Avogadro's law: at constant T and V, P is directly proportional to n, so doubling n doubles P.

tasks.question: Double both the temperature and the volume. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Temperature to 600 K and Volume to 49.0 L.
tasks.hint: T doubles, which doubles P. V doubles, which halves P. Do the two effects cancel?
tasks.why: P = nR(2T)/(2V) = nRT/V, so the two changes cancel exactly and the pressure is unchanged.

title: Boyle and Charles — One Change at a Time
concept: Boyle's law, Charles's law and Gay-Lussac's law as special cases of P = nRT/V
prompt: Watch the pressure as you change temperature and volume, then predict the factor.
learning_objective: Read a proportionality off the ideal gas law and state it as a multiplier.
reference: PhET Gas Properties; ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Ideal Gas Law'
note: The particle speed is drawn proportional to the square root of the temperature, which is the correct scaling for the rms molecular speed.

spec.title: Boyle and Charles — One Change at a Time
spec.instruction: Set the sliders, then choose what happens to the pressure and press Check.
spec.unit_note: P = nRT/V, with P in kPa, V in L, T in K, n in mol and R = 8.314 J/mol/K.

tasks.question: Double the volume at constant temperature. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Volume to 49.0 L and leave Temperature at 300 K.
tasks.hint: V is in the denominator, so a bigger V gives a smaller P.
tasks.why: Boyle's law: P falls to half. 101.8 kPa at 24.5 L becomes 50.9 kPa at 49.0 L.

tasks.question: Halve the temperature at constant volume. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Temperature to 150 K and leave Volume at 24.5 L.
tasks.hint: T is in the numerator, so cooling the gas lowers the pressure.
tasks.why: P is directly proportional to T at constant n and V, so halving T halves P: 101.8 kPa becomes 50.9 kPa.

tasks.question: Triple the temperature at constant volume. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Temperature to 900 K and leave Volume at 24.5 L.
tasks.hint: T is in the numerator. If T goes up by a factor of three, so does P.
tasks.why: P is directly proportional to T, so tripling T triples P: 101.8 kPa becomes 305.4 kPa.

tasks.question: Quarter the volume at constant temperature. What happens to the pressure?
tasks.setup: Set Volume to 6.125 L and leave Temperature at 300 K.
tasks.hint: Shrinking V by a factor of four multiplies P by four.
tasks.why: P is inversely proportional to V, so dividing V by four multiplies P by four: 101.8 kPa becomes 407.2 kPa.

title: Ohm's Law — Two Resistors in Series
concept: Series resistance, current and voltage drop (I = V/R)
prompt: Set the supply voltage, read the ammeter, then commit to what Ohm's law predicts.
learning_objective: Add series resistances, apply I = V/R, and use V = IR to say which resistor takes the larger potential difference.
reference: PhET Circuit Construction Kit; ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Circuits'
note: The voltage drop across each resistor is hidden until you commit, so 'which resistor drops the most' is a prediction and not a lookup.

spec.title: Ohm's Law — Two Resistors in Series
spec.instruction: Move the supply slider to explore, then answer and press Check.
spec.note: Ideal wires, ideal ammeter, and a battery with no internal resistance.

tasks.question: What is the total resistance of R1 = 2 Ω and R2 = 4 Ω in series?
tasks.hint: In series the resistances simply add: R_total = R1 + R2.
tasks.why: Series resistances add, so R_total = 2 Ω + 4 Ω = 6 Ω.

tasks.question: With R1 = 2 Ω and R2 = 4 Ω in series, what current flows when the supply is 6.0 V?
tasks.hint: Find the total resistance first, then use I = V / R_total.

tasks.question: What current flows when the supply is raised to 12.0 V, with the same two resistors?
tasks.hint: The resistance has not changed. Doubling the voltage doubles the current.
tasks.why: I = 12.0 / 6 = 2.00 A. At constant resistance the current is proportional to the voltage.

tasks.question: The same current passes through both resistors. Which one has the larger potential difference across it?
tasks.hint: V = IR. With I the same in both, the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the supply.
tasks.why: At 1.00 A, R1 drops 2.0 V and R2 drops 4.0 V. In series the drops always add back up to the supply voltage, and the largest resistance takes the largest share.

title: Ohm's Law — Three Resistors in Series
concept: Total resistance and current in a three-resistor series circuit
prompt: Three resistors in one loop: work out the total, then the current, then which resistor takes the most voltage.
learning_objective: Combine three series resistances and use them to predict current and voltage distribution.
reference: PhET Circuit Construction Kit; ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Circuits'
note: The voltage drop across each resistor is hidden until you commit.

spec.title: Ohm's Law — Three Resistors in Series
spec.instruction: Set the supply, then answer and press Check.
spec.note: Ideal wires and ammeter; the battery has no internal resistance.

tasks.question: What is the total resistance of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω in series?
tasks.hint: Add all three resistances.

tasks.question: What current flows from a 10.0 V supply through this 20 Ω series combination?
tasks.hint: I = V / R_total.

tasks.question: Which of the three resistors has the largest potential difference across it?
tasks.hint: V = IR and I is the same everywhere in a series loop.
tasks.why: At 0.50 A the drops are 2.0 V, 3.0 V and 5.0 V, which add to 10.0 V. The 10 Ω resistor takes the largest share.

tasks.question: What current flows when the supply is raised to 12.0 V?
tasks.hint: Same 20 Ω, higher voltage.

title: Balancing Combustion Equations
concept: Conservation of atoms and stoichiometric coefficients
prompt: Step the coefficients until every element has the same count on both sides, using the smallest whole numbers.
learning_objective: Balance a combustion equation by conserving each element and reduce to the lowest whole-number coefficients.
reference: PhET Balancing Chemical Equations; ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Balancing Chemical Equations'
note: The atom counts are computed from the formula text, so they are exactly what each formula implies.

spec.title: Balancing Combustion Equations
spec.instruction: Use the − and + buttons to change each coefficient. The counts update live; press Check when every element matches.
spec.note: Atoms are conserved: the count of each element must be the same on both sides.

equations.why: 1 C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Three carbons need three CO2; eight hydrogens need four H2O; that leaves 10 oxygens to supply, so five O2.
1 Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2. Two irons need two Fe, and the three oxygens carried away by CO require three CO.

title: Balancing Equations — AP Chemistry Set
concept: Balancing equations with polyatomic ions and nested groups
prompt: Balance each equation with the lowest whole-number coefficients, including formulas with parentheses.
learning_objective: Balance equations containing nested groups such as Ca(OH)2 and Ca3(PO4)2 by conserving every element.
reference: PhET Balancing Chemical Equations; AP Chemistry Unit 4 stoichiometry
note: A group in brackets, such as OH in Ca(OH)2, is multiplied by the subscript after the bracket.

spec.title: Balancing Equations — AP Chemistry Set
spec.instruction: Step the coefficients until every element matches on both sides, at the lowest whole numbers.
spec.note: Count the atoms inside brackets first, then multiply by the subscript after the bracket: Ca(OH)2 has 2 O and 2 H.

equations.why: 3 Ca(OH)2 + 2 H3PO4 -> 1 Ca3(PO4)2 + 6 H2O. Three calcium need three Ca(OH)2; two phosphate groups need two H3PO4; the 12 hydrogens that leaves make six H2O.
2 Al + 6 HCl -> 2 AlCl3 + 3 H2. Each AlCl3 takes three chlorines, so two AlCl3 need six HCl, which release three H2.
1 Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2. The three oxygens in Fe2O3 are each removed by one CO, giving three CO2.

title: Titration — Strong Acid with Strong Base
concept: pH curve for a strong acid / strong base titration and the equivalence point
prompt: Add titrant and watch the pH curve turn. Read the equivalence point off the plot, then commit.
learning_objective: Locate the equivalence point from the steep part of the curve and predict pH from the excess strong acid or base.
reference: ExploreLearning Gizmos 'Titration'; AP Chemistry Unit 8 acids and bases
note: Strong acid / strong base model: water autoionisation is neglected, so the curve passes exactly through pH 7.00 at the equivalence point instead of rounding the corner.

spec.title: Titration — Strong Acid with Strong Base
spec.instruction: Add titrant with the buttons or drag the playhead. Answer the question, then press Check.
spec.note: Model: strong acid + strong base. Water autoionisation is neglected, so pH is exactly 7.00 at the equivalence point.

tasks.question: Add titrant until the curve turns sharply. At what volume of NaOH does the equivalence point occur?
tasks.hint: The equivalence point is where the curve is steepest — the middle of the near-vertical jump.
tasks.why: At equivalence the moles of base added equal the moles of acid: 0.100 M x 25.0 mL = 0.100 M x V, so V = 25.0 mL.

tasks.question: Predict the pH after 12.5 mL of NaOH has been added — half of the acid is neutralised.
tasks.hint: You have neutralised half the acid, so half of it is still there as free H+. That is still a fairly acidic solution.
tasks.why: 1.25 mmol of H+ remains in a total volume of 37.5 mL, so [H+] = 0.0333 M and pH = -log10(0.0333) = 1.48. Half-neutralising a strong acid does not give pH 7.

tasks.question: Predict the pH exactly at the equivalence point.
tasks.hint: A strong acid and a strong base neutralise to give a neutral salt solution.
tasks.why: At equivalence every H+ has been matched by an OH-. Only NaCl and water remain, so the pH is 7.00.

tasks.question: Predict the pH after 30.0 mL of NaOH has been added, well past the equivalence point.
tasks.hint: Past equivalence the pH is set by the excess strong base, so work out [OH-] and convert.
tasks.why: Excess base = 0.100 M x 5.0 mL = 0.50 mmol in 55.0 mL, so [OH-] = 0.00909 M, pOH = 2.04 and pH = 11.96.

title: Titration — Dilute Acid, Concentrated Base
concept: Equivalence volume when the acid and base concentrations differ
prompt: The acid is weaker in concentration than the base. Add titrant, find the jump, and predict the pH at two points.
learning_objective: Compute the equivalence volume from moles and predict pH before and after equivalence.
note: Strong acid / strong base model: water autoionisation is neglected, so pH is exactly 7.00 at the equivalence point.

spec.title: Titration — Dilute Acid, Concentrated Base
spec.instruction: Add titrant with the buttons or drag the playhead, then answer and press Check.
spec.note: Model: strong acid + strong base. Water autoionisation is neglected, so pH is exactly 7.00 at equivalence.

tasks.question: At what volume of NaOH does the equivalence point occur?
tasks.hint: The base is twice as concentrated as the acid, so you need less of it. Match the moles, not the volumes.
tasks.why: Moles of acid = 0.050 M x 20.0 mL = 1.00 mmol. That needs 1.00 mmol of base, which is 1.00 / 0.100 = 10.0 mL of NaOH.

tasks.question: Predict the pH after 5.0 mL of NaOH has been added.
tasks.hint: You have neutralised only a quarter of the acid. Most of the H+ is still free.
tasks.why: 0.50 mmol of H+ remains in 25.0 mL, so [H+] = 0.020 M and pH = -log10(0.020) = 1.70.

tasks.question: Predict the pH after 15.0 mL of NaOH has been added.
tasks.hint: That is 5.0 mL past equivalence, so the pH is set by the excess strong base.
tasks.why: Excess base = 0.100 M x 5.0 mL = 0.50 mmol in 35.0 mL, so [OH-] = 0.01429 M, pOH = 1.85 and pH = 12.15.

tasks.question: Predict the pH after 20.0 mL of NaOH has been added.
tasks.hint: Twice the titrant of the equivalence point, so twice the excess base.
tasks.why: Excess base = 0.100 M x 10.0 mL = 1.00 mmol in 40.0 mL, so [OH-] = 0.025 M, pOH = 1.60 and pH = 12.40.
